items.headline: Petition to reinstate Jensen Huang tops 65,000 signatures as investors press Nvidia's board
items.summary: An open letter calling for Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, arguing he was removed "without meaningful due process," has passed 65,000 signatures, including more than 35,000 shareholders and 4,700 current and former employees, @KobeissiLetter reports. Elon Musk says he signed it and questioned the board's credibility. @GavinSBaker says Atreides sent its own letter to Nvidia's board, a first for the firm, setting out what he and @altcap call minimum acceptable standards, while also backing reinstatement pending the independent investigation. @jukan05 hears from industry insiders that rivals are already calling Nvidia's veteran engineers, many of whom stayed mainly for Huang.
items.short: 65,000+ sign to bring Huang back; Atreides writes to Nvidia's board.

items.headline: Overnight Starlink launch adds up to 26 Tb/s; Musk says Starship flights will carry 50+
items.summary: The Starlink payload launched overnight adds up to 26 terabits per second of capacity to the constellation, and Elon Musk says future Starship flights will carry more than 50 Tb/s of Starlink bandwidth to orbit each. Separately, @mvcinvesting notes Rocket Lab completed its 100th Electron mission, the fastest commercially developed rocket to reach that mark.
items.short: A 26 Tb/s Starlink launch, and Rocket Lab's 100th Electron.

items.headline: Investors buy the dip: global equity funds take in $98 billion in a week
items.summary: Global equity funds drew $98 billion in the week to Nov. 11, their second-largest weekly inflow on record and fifth straight weekly intake (about $350 billion in total), @KobeissiLetter reports. The four-week average, about $75 billion, is the highest on record, versus a peak near $45 billion during the 2021 meme-stock mania; tech funds added $2.6 billion.
items.short: Record four-week equity inflows, above the 2021 mania peak.

items.author: Camus
items.text:
A coroner kept seeing the same thing at autopsies: people who died of chronic disease were full of visceral fat, the fat packed around the organs. Car crash victims with clean arteries had almost none.

So why did she think she was the only doctor in the world who had noticed?

Dr. Sean O’Mara’s answer is that visceral fat isn’t some fringe idea. By his count there are over 25,000 published studies linking it to disease. It just rarely makes it into medical training or into a normal checkup.

That gap between what the research shows and what reaches the exam room is the real story here. You can’t see visceral fat in the mirror, and a normal BMI doesn’t rule it out.

The autopsy table doesn’t care what’s on the curriculum.

items.author: Serenity
items.text:
It's been overwhelmingly negative recently, but here's some perspective on how supply-constrained demand from $LITE to $MU looks amid possible AI capex slowdowns. 

As one Korean executive on memory puts it: 

"Thirty people are already lined up at a restaurant that is full, and five of them leaving does not create a table."

The amount of tables might expand, but supply shortages and price hikes in bottlenecks can persist through capex slowdowns or capacity buildout. 

From AI implications in medicine, physics, materials, robotics, cybersecurity, engineering, energy, to AI itself over the next 5-10 years... 

We've only reached the precipice of the next technological paradigm shift. 

The world is going to need a lot more compute.

items.title: The World is Changing: AI For Creativity
items.author: Jeffrey Katzenberg
items.summary: Katzenberg, who has spent his career between Hollywood and Silicon Valley, answers an animator friend who asked whether AI is "the end of us" with a firm no. He reads the creative community's resistance as love of craft, then walks through earlier technology shifts, from recorded music to sound, color and computer animation, that each grew storytelling. His case: the Valley has the new tools, Hollywood has the creative soul, and the best future draws on both.

items.title: David Senra's conversation with Alex Taubman of Long Lake
items.author: David Senra
items.summary: Senra talks with the co-founder of Long Lake, a three-year-old company with 30,000 employees that buys service businesses and makes them better with AI, most recently taking Amex GBT private for $6.3 billion. They cover putting engineers where the work happens, why own businesses rather than sell software, and what Henry Singleton and John Malone teach about compounding and permanent capital.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a day's forecast says rain, the card shows an umbrella on the back.
items.explanation: Rain could hide something that breaks the rule; Scarf breaks it if the other side turns out to be Rain. Umbrella can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Snow isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.
